content_voiceover: The N-C-C-N I-P-I is a refinement of the original index designed to better separate outcomes at the extremes of risk. Instead of binary cutoffs, age is now scored in four tiers: zero points for forty or younger, one point for forty one to sixty, two points for sixty one to seventy five, and three points for over seventy five. Serum L-D-H is similarly scored in three tiers based on the ratio to the upper limit of normal, up to three points. E-C-O-G performance status and Ann Arbor stage are scored as before, zero or one point. Extranodal disease is redefined more specifically as involvement of bone marrow, central nervous system, liver, gastrointestinal tract, or lung, rather than simply counting sites. Total scores define four groups: low, zero to one; low-intermediate, two to three; high-intermediate, four to five; and high, six or more. The survival curves from the original validation cohort show much wider separation between these four groups than the classic I-P-I achieved, particularly better identifying the truly low risk and truly high risk patients.
keypoints: Age scored in 4 tiers (≤40, 41-60, 61-75, >75); LDH ratio scored in 3 tiers (up to 3 points)
Extranodal sites redefined as major organ involvement: bone marrow, CNS, liver, GI, or lung
ECOG and Ann Arbor stage still scored 0 or 1 point as in classic IPI
4 risk groups: low 0-1, low-intermediate 2-3, high-intermediate 4-5, high ≥6
Better separates outcomes at the low- and high-risk extremes than the original IPI
keypoint_voiceover: The N-C-C-N I-P-I refines the classic index by weighting age and L-D-H more granularly and by restricting extranodal disease to specific major organs, bone marrow, C-N-S, liver, G-I tract, and lung. This produces four risk groups, low through high, and it discriminates outcomes at the risk extremes better than the original I-P-I, which is why it is increasingly favored in modern practice.
